chapter_theme: On Manipallavam the guardian goddess Deepathilakai meets Manimekalai, who answers 'who are you?' with her two births; the bowl Amudhasurabhi rises into her hand on the Buddha's day, Deepathilakai preaches that those who feed the hungry give life, Manimekalai names the bowl as the fruit of a meal she gave a holy man in her former life, and she flies home to name Madhavi and Sudhamathi as her sisters of that life.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, in her former birth Lakshmi, wife of Rahulan
the guardian goddess of the jewel seat on Manipallavam, set there by Indra
the Buddha, the Lord of the Bodhi tree, praised and addressed but not present
Manimekalai's mother, in a former birth her elder sister Tharai
Manimekalai's companion, in a former birth her elder sister Veerai

manimekalai:11:1-8.unit_note: Boundary moved from 10 to 8: Deepathilakai's question closes with என்றலும் at 8; Manimekalai's answer begins at 9 and the core unit 11-20 cut it after its first two lines.
manimekalai:11:1-8.reading: Left alone on Manipallavam after the goddess has gone, Manimekalai looks over its white sand hills, groves and pools and wanders a kaatham, until Deepathilakai appears in a deity's form and asks who she is, come here like a woman cast up from a wrecked ship.
manimekalai:11:1-8.nuance: The question 'who are you?' (யார் நீ, 8) is the hinge of the kaathai: Manimekalai will answer it with two births, not one name.
manimekalai:11:1-8.event: Manimekalai wanders the island and the goddess Deepathilakai appears and asks who she is.

manimekalai:11:9-20.unit_note: Boundary moved from 10 to 8 at the start: the unit now opens with Manimekalai's answer at 9 and keeps its original end at 20, where the narration turns to Deepathilakai.
manimekalai:11:9-20.reading: Manimekalai answers by asking in which birth the question is meant: in the birth gone by she was Lakshmi, wife of the prince Rahulan, and in this one she is Manimekalai, Madhavi's daughter, brought here by the goddess of her name to know her birth at the jewel seat; then she asks Deepathilakai the same question.
manimekalai:11:9-20.nuance: Her reply turns a request for identity into a doctrine of identity: the self who answers spans two lives (போய பிறவியில் ... ஆய பிறவியில், 11, 13), and she names the coming and its use (வரவு, பயன், 17) as if reporting an errand completed.
manimekalai:11:9-20.event: Manimekalai tells Deepathilakai she was Lakshmi, Rahulan's wife, in her former birth and is now Madhavi's daughter, and asks who Deepathilakai is.

claims.claim: one person continues across births, and the jewel seat lets her know her former birth

manimekalai:11:21-36.unit_note: Boundary moved from 43 to 36: Deepathilakai's account of herself and of who may see the seat closes with இது கேள் at 36; the description of the Gomukhi pool and the bowl that follows begins at 37 and runs into the core unit 44-58.
manimekalai:11:21-36.reading: Deepathilakai says she has come from worshipping the feet of the Lord of dharma on the peak of Samantam in the Jewel Island, feet that are a ship of dharma across the great sea of births, and that she guards this jewel seat at the command of the king of the gods; those who keep unswervingly the vow of the dharma the Lord taught, on seeing and worshipping it, come to know their former births, and such people are rare.
manimekalai:11:21-36.nuance: The gods are put in service to the Buddha's seat: Indra (தேவர் கோன், 28) assigns the guard, and the guardian goddess herself is a pilgrim to the footprint. Lines 34-35 are compressed: the word of dharma is said to be fitting in the world for those rare ones, which may mean that only they are fit to receive teaching.
manimekalai:11:21-36.event: Deepathilakai names herself as the seat's guardian, set there by Indra, newly come from worshipping the Buddha's feet on Samantam.

claims.claim: the Buddha's feet are a ship that carries beings off the great sea of births
those who keep the vow of the Buddha's dharma and worship the seat come to know their former births

manimekalai:11:37-58.unit_note: Boundary moved from 43 to 36 at the start: the unit now opens on the Gomukhi pool at 37 and keeps its original end at 58, where the bowl enters Manimekalai's hand.
manimekalai:11:37-58.reading: Deepathilakai tells of the pool Gomukhi before the seat, where each year on the day the Lord of the Bodhi appeared the great bowl Amudhasurabhi of Aputhiran rises, and says that day and hour have come round now as if for her; the life-medicine put in it never fails and only tires the hands of those who take, and Aravanan in her town will tell her its nature; Manimekalai worships the seat, circles the pool with the goddess, and the bowl comes into her hand.
manimekalai:11:37-58.nuance: Lines 40-43 fix the day by season and stars (spring, the sun in Taurus, a count of thirteen days, the middle star); the reckoning is compressed and I cannot fix it, beyond its tie to the Buddha's day (போதித் தலைவனொடு பொருந்தித் தோன்றும், 43). The food is called ஆருயிர்மருந்து, medicine for dear life, and the only limit on the bowl is the tiredness of the receivers' hands (49), so scarcity moves from the giver to the taker.
manimekalai:11:37-58.event: Deepathilakai tells of Aputhiran's bowl rising from the Gomukhi pool; Manimekalai worships and circles the pool, and the bowl rises into her hand.

manimekalai:11:59-75.unit_note: Boundary moved from 73 to 75: the sentence that begins with என்ற ஆய் இழை முன்னர் at 72 runs through the Lord who appears in the Bodhi's shade (73-74) to its verb உரைக்கும் at 75; the core unit cut it at 73.
manimekalai:11:59-75.reading: Overjoyed at receiving the bowl, Manimekalai praises the Buddha's feet line by line, as the hero who conquered Mara, who drove off the enmity of evil ways, who strives for others' dharma, who did not want heaven, who went beyond reckoning, who gives others sight, whose ears are shut to evil words and whose tongue excels in truth, who walks to end the pain of the hell-dwellers and the serpents, and says her tongue can only bow, not praise; Deepathilakai praises the same feet and turns to speak.
manimekalai:11:59-75.nuance: The praise is a litany with the refrain நின் அடி closing ten lines; its first item, மாரனை வெல்லும் வீர (61), names desire's god as the one enemy, and துறக்கம் வேண்டாத் (64) sets the Buddha against the heaven that Vedic and Jain merit aims at. The gift of the bowl is answered not by thanks to the goddess but by praise of the teacher.
manimekalai:11:59-75.event: Manimekalai, holding the bowl, praises the Buddha's feet, and Deepathilakai praises them and begins to speak to her.

claims.claim: the Buddha conquered Mara and, not desiring heaven, strives for the dharma of others

manimekalai:11:76-98.unit_note: Boundary moved from 74 to 76 at the start and from 91 to 98 at the end: Deepathilakai's speech begins at 76 after உரைக்கும் (75) and runs to கண்டனை என்றலும் at 98; the core unit 92-115 cut it before its maxim.
manimekalai:11:76-98.reading: Deepathilakai says her tongue cannot rise to praise those who cure the sinner hunger, which destroys high birth, kills dignity, drops the raft of learning, strips modesty and beauty and leaves a man standing at others' gates with his wife; she recalls a drought in which a Brahmin of the Veda, wandering, was about to eat dog's flesh until the god appeared and gave rain; those who give to the able sell dharma, the world's true way belongs to those who end the hunger of the helpless, those who give food give life, and Manimekalai, having taken up that gift of life, has seen flawless dharma.
manimekalai:11:76-98.nuance: Line 96 is Purananuru 18's உண்டி கொடுத்தோர் உயிர்கொடுத் தோரே, a king's counsel to build tanks, here made the creed of an alms-bowl; and kaathai 10:90 has already lent the same poem's உணவின் பிண்டம். The famine tale (82-91) is compressed: அரசு தலைநீங்கிய (84) may be a Brahmin who had left kingship or a land without a king, and the one who performs Indra's rite (88) may be that Brahmin; I read it as the old tale of a hungry sage at a dog's flesh, but the lines do not name him. Line 92 classes gifts to those who can repay as trade in dharma.
manimekalai:11:76-98.event: Deepathilakai tells Manimekalai that those who cure hunger are beyond praise and that in taking the bowl she has seen true dharma.

claims.claim: hunger destroys birth, dignity, learning, modesty and beauty
giving to those able to repay is selling dharma; the true way is to end the hunger of the helpless
those who give food give life

manimekalai:11:99-123.unit_note: Boundary moved from 92 to 99 at the start and from 115 to 123 at the end: Manimekalai's reply runs from 99 to வேட்கையேன் என at 118, and Deepathilakai's answer closes with என்று அவள் உரைப்ப at 123; the core units broke her reply at 115 in the middle of its simile.
manimekalai:11:99-123.reading: Manimekalai says that in the birth she left, when her husband was dying of the sight-venom and she was about to burn with him, she fell into a dream-like daze like the hour she fed Saathusakkaran, and that deed's fruit has now come to her hand as this bowl; she longs to see its food flow, like a mother's breast at the face of her newborn, for the many who stand ragged at the gates of those enjoying the fruit of dharma sown in this land; Deepathilakai says she herself had forgotten that nature, that the bowl flows truly only for the excellent who feed out of compassion with dharma as witness, and bids her rise.
manimekalai:11:99-123.nuance: Karma is on both sides of the gate: the prosperous enjoy the fruit of dharma sown (108-109), and those outside are, on one reading of 112-113, those who did not stand by dharma before; yet the speaker's response to this is the mother's milk, not a verdict. Line 101 (உயிரொடு வேவேன்) and the run 111-113 are compressed and my reading of them is not secure. The bowl's condition (120-121) is the condition Aputhiran set when he let it go (14:93-94).
manimekalai:11:99-123.event: Manimekalai tells that the bowl is the fruit of her feeding Saathusakkaran in her former birth and longs to feed the hungry with it; Deepathilakai says it flows only for the compassionate and bids her rise.

claims.claim: a gift to a holy man in a former birth ripens as a means of giving in this one
the prosperous enjoy the fruit of dharma sown before
the bowl yields only for those who feed out of compassion, with dharma as witness

manimekalai:11:124-146.unit_note: Boundary moved from 129 to 123 at the start: the narration of Manimekalai's departure starts at 124 and the core unit 116-129 broke Madhavi's cry (128-130) across two units at a break score of 0. The unit ends at the kaathai's close, 146.
manimekalai:11:124-146.reading: Manimekalai bows at Deepathilakai's feet, takes the bowl, worships the seat and rises through the sky, appearing before Madhavi just as she cries that the seventh day the true goddess promised has come and her daughter has not; she clears their bewilderment, hails Madhavi and Sudhamathi as Tharai and Veerai, her elder sisters in the birth when all three were born of Amudhapathi, who have now become her mothers, bids them seek from Aravana Adigal the austerity that cuts evil deeds in this human body, and has them worship the bowl, and they set out for the teacher.
manimekalai:11:124-146.nuance: The recognition reverses kinship: her elder sisters of the last birth are her mothers in this one (அவ்வையர் ஆயினீர், 137). The human body is named as the place where austerity can cut evil deeds (138-139), the first time in the kaathai the bowl's dharma of feeding is joined to a path of release.
manimekalai:11:124-146.event: Manimekalai flies home with the bowl, finds Madhavi grieving at the seventh day, tells her and Sudhamathi they were her sisters Tharai and Veerai, has them worship the bowl, and they set out for Aravana Adigal.

claims.claim: austerity that cuts evil deeds is to be undertaken while one has a human body

links.note: Aputhiran, stranded on Manipallavam, let the bowl into Gomukhi bidding it rise once a year and enter the hand of anyone who keeps compassion and guards lives; here it rises into Manimekalai's hand on that day.
links.teaches: The bowl's arrival is not a goddess's gift but the meeting of a condition laid down by its last owner, so the kaathai tests Manimekalai before the reader is told what the test was.

links.note: Deepathilakai says Aravanan will tell Manimekalai the bowl's nature (52); in the next kaathai Aravana Adigal says she has the bowl and gives the one dharma common to men and gods, curing hunger.
links.teaches: The goddess hands over the object and defers its meaning to a human teacher, so the epic places authority over the bowl's use with the Buddhist monk rather than the island's deity.

links.note: The Naladiyar's ascetic's bowl (தவசி கடிஞை) is filled slowly at door after door by householders' small gifts; Manimekalai's bowl, held by a renunciant, never fails and only the takers' hands tire.
links.teaches: Set together, the two bowls reverse the flow between householder and ascetic: the quatrain's begging bowl is the image of a giver's merit filling, while the epic's is an ascetic's vessel that gives without end.

gains.a: the bowl's inexhaustibility is seen against the ordinary begging bowl it inverts, which the epic never needs to describe
gains.b: the quatrain's image of the slowly filled bowl gains its opposite, which shows that its point is about the giver's accumulation, not the bowl

links.note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; Deepathilakai calls the feet of the Lord of dharma on Samantam the ship of dharma that frees from the great sea called birth (23-25).
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic takes the Kural's unnamed Lord and his feet as the Buddha's footprint on a named peak and turns swimming into being carried by a ship, so the couplet's open theism becomes a pilgrimage relic served by the gods.

gains.a: Deepathilakai's image is shown to rest on the Kural's opening chapter, giving the Buddhist claim the Kural's wording of release
gains.b: the couplet's இறைவன் is shown open to sectarian claiming, read here by a Buddhist work as the Buddha

links.note: Purananuru 18 tells a Pandya king that those who give food give life (உண்டி கொடுத்தோர் உயிர்கொடுத் தோரே) and that land waiting on the sky does not serve its ruler, so he must build tanks; Deepathilakai gives the same line (96) after a famine ended only by a god's rain.
links.teaches: The maxim moves from a king's public works to a renunciant's alms-bowl, and the remedy for a failing sky moves from tanks a ruler digs to a god's gift and a bowl that never empties.

gains.a: line 96 is shown to be a borrowed Sangam maxim, so the goddess's sermon carries the authority of old royal counsel
gains.b: the poem's maxim gains a later life in which the duty to feed passes from the state to a single compassionate giver

links.note: Kural 225 ranks the strength of those who endure hunger, read by its commentators as ascetics, below that of those who remove it; here a goddess tells a girl who has just renounced that removing hunger is beyond praise and the true way of the world.
links.teaches: The epic dissolves the couplet's ranking of giver over ascetic by putting the bowl in a renunciant's hand, so the one who endures hunger becomes the one who ends it.

gains.a: the sermon's praise of the hunger-curer is seen as an answer to the Kural's ranking, not only a commonplace
gains.b: the couplet's opposition between ascetic and giver is shown not to be fixed, since a renunciant may be the giver

links.note: Kural 1042 calls poverty 'a sinner' (இன்மை எனவொரு பாவி) that comes with this world and the next both lost; Deepathilakai calls hunger 'the sinner' (பசிப் பிணி என்னும் பாவி, 80) that destroys birth, learning, modesty and beauty.
links.teaches: The Kural speaks to the poor man about what poverty takes from him, even merit for the next world; the epic speaks to the one who can cure it, so the merit the poor man loses becomes the giver's highest dharma.

gains.a: the list of hunger's ravages is seen to extend a Kural formula, which places the sermon within the ethics books' account of want
gains.b: the couplet's loss of the next world gains a remedy outside the poor man, in another's gift

links.note: The goddess told Lakshmi that the dharma of the meal Saathusakkaran ate would not leave her and would end her births; here Manimekalai names this bowl as that meal's fruit (105-106).
links.teaches: The prophecy's fruit arrives first not as release but as a means of further giving, so in the epic merit ripens into the power to make more merit before it ends births.

links.note: The Naladiyar calls liberality milk a cow yields gladly to its calf, against the base who yield only when squeezed; Manimekalai wants the bowl to flow at the hungry's faces as a mother's breast flows at her newborn's (114-118), and Deepathilakai says it flows only for those who feed from compassion (120-121).
links.teaches: The epic turns the quatrain's distinction between glad and forced giving into a property of the vessel itself, which will not yield to a giver whose gift is not compassion.

gains.a: the mother's-breast simile and the bowl's condition are seen to rest on an old ethics image of giving as lactation
gains.b: the quatrain's moral distinction gains a story in which the manner of giving decides whether anything is given at all

links.note: Tirumular says joy and sorrow are settled by former deeds and that those who see their joy and still do not give know no dharma; Manimekalai sees the prosperous enjoying the fruit of dharma sown (108-109) while the hungry stand ragged at their gates.
links.teaches: A Saiva and a Buddhist text agree that karma explaining who is fed does not excuse withholding, and the epic adds that the giver's own gift is the deed that will return as a means of giving.

gains.a: the unit's view of the rich at their gates is seen to be shared doctrine across the schools, not a Buddhist peculiarity
gains.b: Tirumular's argument gains a case in which the deed of giving returns, the bowl that is the fruit of a past meal

links.note: The goddess told Sudhamathi, as Veerai, Tharai's younger sister, that in seven days Lakshmi would return knowing her birth; Madhavi cries that the seventh day has come and Manimekalai arrives to name Tharai and Veerai.
links.teaches: The promise and its keeping frame Manimekalai's island journey as a timed rebirth-recognition, and Madhavi's near loss of faith on the last day sets the goddess's truthfulness against a mother's fear.

new_concepts.gloss: the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: பிறழா நோன்பினர் (31)

source_issues: The core unit boundary at 129/130 has break score 0 and splits Madhavi's cry (128-130); moved in this file.
Lines 40-43 give the day of the bowl's rising in compressed calendrical terms (எரி கதிர் இடபத்து, ஒருபதின் மேலும் ஒருமூன்று, மீனத்து இடைநிலை மீனத்து) that I cannot fix.
